Voiced alveolar lateral [l] plus front rounded [y], the Greek upsilon sound
Bilabial nasal [m] plus voiceless stop [p] and voiceless fricative [s]; the final cluster is -mps

pronunciation.approximation: 'OH-lu-poss' — the first syllable is short and stressed, the 'y' is rounded like French u, and the name ends in a crisp 'poss'.

pronunciation.note: Ólympos is accent-preserving Tier 2: the acute on the first omicron marks stress, but the word contains no long vowel. The name may be pre-Greek; its etymology from *ol-um- 'luminous' is speculative, so the pronunciation follows the attested Greek form rather than a reconstructed prototype.

domains.title: Mountain of the Gods
domains.subtitle: The domain of Ólympos
domains.lead: Ólympos is the mountain that rules: the highest peak of Greece became, in epic imagination, the bronze-floored palace of the Olympian gods — seat of Zeus's council, storehouse of his thunderbolts, and the fixed point from which the whole cosmos is governed. To call anything 'Olympian' is still to call it supreme.

cards.name: Palace of the Gods
cards.desc: Zeus's bronze-floored hall, Hera's golden throne, and Hephaestus's forges crown the mountain above the clouds.

cards.name: Omphalos
cards.desc: The navel stone at Delphi, not Olympus itself, marked the earth's center, but Olympus was its celestial counterpart.

cards.name: Throne of the Olympians
cards.desc: After the Titanomachy, Olympus became the seat of the victorious gods who divided the cosmos by lot.

cards.name: Pindar's Bright Seat
cards.desc: Poets placed Olympus above storm and cloud, a luminous court accessible only to the deathless gods.

mythology.lead: Ólympos is the mountain that became a palace, the palace that became a government, and the government that became a metaphor for supreme authority. Homer places the gods on its cloud-hidden summit, feasting on ambrosia while the Muses sing; Hesiod makes it the muster-ground of the war against the Titans. Ancient Greeks knew several peaks named Ólympos, but the Thessalian mountain — the highest in Greece — became canonical, and its poets set the divine court just above the snowline: a real place, and never quite reachable.

myths.title: The Palace of the Gods
myths.text:
Homer's Olympus is not merely a high mountain in Thessaly but the fixed abode of the Olympian gods, hidden from mortal sight by unbroken clouds. There Zeus has his bronze-floored hall, Hera her golden throne, and Hephaestus his forges. The gods gather in council on its summit, debate the fates of cities, and receive the prayers of mortals through rising sacrificial smoke.

The mountain is therefore both a real place and a cosmic location. Pilgrims might look toward the actual Mount Olympus from the plains of Thessaly, but poets located the divine court just above its peak, in a realm where snow never melts and the light is always clear. This double existence made Olympus the perfect symbol of transcendent power rooted in recognizable geography.

myths.title: The Fall of the Titans
myths.text:
After Zeus and his siblings defeated the Titans, Olympus became the seat of the new regime. The defeated Titans were cast into Tartarus, while the victorious gods divided the cosmos by lot: Zeus received sky and Olympus, Poseidon the sea, and Hades the underworld. The mountain thus marks the boundary between the ordered present and the defeated chaos of the older gods.

Hesiod describes Olympus as the place from which the Olympians marched to war and to which they returned in triumph. Its gates are guarded by the Horai, and its heights are inaccessible to those who have not sworn allegiance to Zeus. To dwell on Olympus is to belong to the victorious order.

myths.title: Hephaestus Thrown from Heaven
myths.text:
Olympus is also the scene of divine discord. In the Iliad, Hera quarrels with Zeus and is hung from the sky by golden fetters; Ares, wounded by Diomedes, howls and flees back to Olympus; and Hephaestus, cast down from heaven by Zeus for defending Hera, falls for a day and lands on Lemnos, crippling him forever. These stories show that Olympus is a court as well as a sanctuary, subject to the same passions and rivalries that trouble mortal houses.

Yet the gods always return to Olympus. Even when they intervene in human wars or descend to the underworld, the mountain remains their home and the seat of their immortality. It is the fixed point around which the changing world turns.

myths.title: Piling Mountains on Mountains
myths.text: Twins once tried to climb into Olympus. Otus and Ephialtes, the Aloadae — boys of nine who grew nine cubits across and nine fathoms tall, 'the tallest and most beautiful mortals after Orion' — threatened the gods themselves: they would pile Ossa on Olympus and Pelion on Ossa, so that the mountains would touch the starry sky, then rule the sea by cutting a canal through it and the land by force, 'without the leave of the gods' (Homer, Odyssey 11.305–320; cf. Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 1.7.4). Artemis destroyed them on Naxos by a ruse — running between them in a deer's shape so that their own spears found each other. The story is the tradition's commentary on its own mountain: Olympus is high not by geology alone but by decree — a wall between mortal and divine that no ambition, however colossal, may legally breach. The twins measured the distance in mountains and came three peaks short.

lore.syncretism: Rome took the mountain over as a word: in Latin verse from Ennius to Ovid, Olympus simply means 'heaven' — the abode of the gods as a region, no peak required — and the borrowing fixed Olympus in every Western language as the generic home of the gods. Christian writers inverted the geography: for the apologists, 'Olympus' became shorthand for the whole fabricated pantheon, and the emptying of the mountain was a favorite proof of the new faith's victory. The Greek world had meanwhile multiplied the name — Mysia, Lycia, Cyprus, and Lesbos each had an Ólympos — which let local cults claim Olympian standing without disputing the Thessalian original. Byzantine monks later retreated to the real mountain's flanks, and when Renaissance painters rebuilt the palace in fresco, they were painting a heaven Rome had already dematerialized.
lore.culturalLegacy: Ólympos is among the most productive names in the modern world — though not always through this mountain. The Olympic Games are named for Olympia in Elis, the sanctuary of Zeus there, not for the gods' home; the two are perpetually confused, and the distinction is itself a lesson in how Greek cult geography worked. The mountain lends its name to the tallest volcano in the solar system (Olympus Mons on Mars) and to an entire camera company that chose the peak as its emblem of aspiration, and to countless hotels and firms trading on its altitude. The mountain itself — summit Mytikas, 2,917 metres — is Greece's first national park, and its climbers knowingly or not retrace the oldest ambition in Europe: to stand where the gods are said to sit.
lore.extendedMeditation: Ólympos solves a problem every religion faces: where does the government sit? The Greeks answered with a real mountain, the highest they could see, and then added that the palace is a little above the peak, in the cloud — near enough to point at, far enough to be unbothered. The mountain is thus the perfect image of legitimate power: geographically rooted, meteorologically aloof. It is also, significantly, a place nobody visits; Olympus has no epic of ascent, only of exclusion — Bellerophon's fall, the Aloadae's failed scaffolding. Authority, the Greeks seem to say, is real, nearby, and permanently off-limits. Every modern 'summit' of leaders, every 'Olympian' calm, every brand that borrows the peak is borrowing that same solution: to be above it all, and visible from everywhere.

lore.archaeology: The divine mountain's real counterpart anchors two rich sites. At its foot lies Díon, the Macedonian sanctuary city of Zeus Olympios — excavated since 1928, with the great temple's colonnades, a Hellenistic theatre, Roman baths, and the mosaics of the villa of Dionysos — the working base of Olympian cult, where Philip II and Alexander staged their victories. High on the mountain, on the plateau of Agios Antonios just below the summits, investigators have identified an ancient open-air sanctuary of Zeus with votive material — the closest archaeology comes to the cloud-hidden palace, proof that someone carried offerings above the treeline to the peak itself. The twelve named summits of the massif — Mytikas highest at 2,917 metres — and the Skala ridge keep the myth legible on the landscape.
